meta.title: Who really said "Honesty is the first chapter in the book of wisdom"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Jefferson. He wrote it to Senator Nathaniel Macon on 12 January 1819 — though his own manuscript reads "1st chapter," not "first."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Honesty is the first chapter in the book of wisdom'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Jefferson — letter to Nathaniel Macon, 12 January 1819. The familiar "first chapter" wording is the reading in the printed editions, Washington's (1853–54) and Ford's (1899).

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1743–1826 · Third U.S. president & drafter of the Declaration of Independence
answer.sourceLine: From a letter Jefferson wrote at Monticello to Senator Nathaniel Macon on 12 January 1819, closing a complaint about bank speculation and worthless paper money. One caveat on the wording: Jefferson’s manuscript reads “honesty is the 1st chapter in the book of wisdom” — the familiar “first” is the reading in the printed editions, H. A. Washington’s (1853–54, vii, 112) and Ford’s (1899, x, 122).

source.heading: The letter to Nathaniel Macon

docMeta.dd: “honesty is the 1st chapter in the book of wisdom”

source.excerpt: but I see nothing in this renewal of the game of ‘Robin’s alive’ but a general demoralization of the nation, a filching from industry it’s honest earnings, wherewith to build up palaces, and raise gambling stock for swindlers and shavers, who are to close too their career of piracies by fraudulent bankruptcies. my dependance for a remedy however, is in the wisdom which grows with time and suffering. whether the succeeding generation is to be more virtuous than their predecessors I cannot say; but I am sure they will have more worldly wisdom, and enough, I hope, to know that honesty is the 1st chapter in the book of wisdom.
trail: 12 January 1819 — Jefferson writes to Senator Nathaniel Macon from Monticello, saying he reads no newspaper but Ritchie’s, “and in that chiefly the advertisements,” and that the one evil which wakes him is that “we have now no measure of value” (full letter at Founders Online ↗). The Thomas Jefferson Foundation’s transcript ↗ carries only the closing passage, and ends it: “honesty is the 1st chapter in the book of wisdom.”

1853–54 — H. A. Washington prints the letter in The Writings of Thomas Jefferson, vol. VII, pages 111–12, and the sentence is already modernised there: “honesty is the first chapter in the book of wisdom.” Scanned volume at the Internet Archive ↗

1899 — Paul Leicester Ford reprints the letter in The Writings of Thomas Jefferson, vol. X (1816–1826), giving the same modernised reading at page 122 — the citation the later reference works pick up. Scanned volume at the Internet Archive ↗

1900 — The Jeffersonian Cyclopedia, edited by John P. Foley, files it as entry 3784 under “Honesty, Wisdom and,” citing “To Nathaniel Macon. vii, 112. Ford ed., x, 122. (M., 1819.)” — “vii, 112” being Washington’s edition and “x, 122” Ford’s. That is how the line entered the reference books. 1900 edition ↗
2019 — Quote Investigator ↗ runs the trace and concludes that Jefferson should receive credit for the words he wrote in the letter dated 12 January 1819.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the manuscript by the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, in Jefferson’s own lowercase orthography. The version everyone quotes — “the first chapter” — is the modernised reading carried by the printed editions, Washington’s of 1853–54 onward.

source.rightsNote: Jefferson wrote the letter in 1819 and died in 1826, so the words themselves are public domain in the United States. The printed editions quoted here — Washington’s Writings of Thomas Jefferson, vol. VII (1853–54), Ford’s vol. X (1899) and The Jeffersonian Cyclopedia (1900) — are all long out of copyright. The manuscript extract above is the Thomas Jefferson Foundation’s transcription; a faithful transcription of a public-domain manuscript adds no new copyright in the US.

author.bio: Thomas Jefferson (13 April 1743 – 4 July 1826) drafted the Declaration of Independence and served as the third president of the United States from 1801 to 1809. He spent his last years at Monticello in Virginia, founding the University of Virginia and writing an enormous volume of letters — the source of most of the sentences now quoted as “Jefferson said.” He died at Monticello on 4 July 1826, fifty years to the day after the Declaration.

misattribution.heading: What actually gets mangled
misattribution.intro: Jefferson is one of the internet’s biggest fake-quote magnets, so suspicion is the right reflex — but this one survives it. What drifts here is the wording and the sourcing, not the author.

items.why: The manuscript, as transcribed by the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, reads “honesty is the 1st chapter in the book of wisdom” in Jefferson’s abbreviated style. The printed editions — Washington’s of 1853–54 and Ford’s of 1899 — both give “first” instead; Quote Investigator notes ↗ that Ford’s transcribed it that way. Same sentence, tidier ordinal.

items.who: Quote pages that print it bare
items.why: The line normally circulates as a free-floating Jefferson aphorism with nothing attached to it. The citation to use has existed since 1900, when The Jeffersonian Cyclopedia ↗ pinned it to “To Nathaniel Macon. vii, 112. Ford ed., x, 122. (M., 1819.)” — Washington’s volume VII and Ford’s volume X.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Jefferson’s own, written at Monticello on 12 January 1819; Quote Investigator ↗ concludes he should receive credit for it.

context.heading: Why he was thinking about honesty
lead: The letter is not a sermon on virtue. It is a retired president complaining about money. Jefferson tells Macon he has stopped following the news, prefers Troy and Lacedaemon to the present day, and has only one grievance that keeps waking him: “we have now no measure of value.” He is being asked eighteen dollars for a yard of broadcloth he used to buy for eighteen shillings, and he can no longer tell where he stands in the scale of property.

From there he turns on the speculators — the “swindlers and shavers” building palaces out of paper and closing their careers in fraudulent bankruptcy. His remedy is not a policy. It is a hope that the next generation will at least be shrewd enough to work out that honesty pays. The sentence now quoted as a moral maxim is, in place, closer to a hard-nosed prediction about finance.
detailsBody: Nathaniel Macon (1757–1837) was a North Carolina Republican, Speaker of the House from 1801 to 1807 and later a U.S. senator. Jefferson called him “Ultimus Romanorum” — the last of the Romans.
context.pull: It is that we have now no measure of value.
